idiom_name: injected java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock strategy with try/finally critical sections
implementation_notes: java.util.concurrent.locks already is the pattern's polymorphic Lock Strategy: an abstract Lock interface (lock, tryLock, lockInterruptibly, unlock) with ReentrantLock and the reader/writer pair ReadWriteLock.readLock()/writeLock() as concrete policies, so the component holds a Lock or a ReadWriteLock chosen at construction and needs no new strategy types. Java has no RAII, so Scoped Locking is emulated with try/finally around every critical section, and the Thread-Safe Interface split (public method locks, private method assumes the lock held) stays a convention because ReentrantLock hides the mistake. Prefer ReentrantLock over the intrinsic monitor when the component may run on virtual threads: on Java 21-23 blocking inside synchronized pins the carrier thread, a restriction JEP 491 removes in Java 24.
pitfalls: unlock() must sit in a finally block: a lock acquired and released outside try/finally survives review and deadlocks only under contention.
ReentrantLock is re-entrant, so a helper that re-locks never deadlocks and never reveals that the component holds the lock twice - only the interface/implementation convention catches it.
Lock is not AutoCloseable, so try-with-resources does not compile for it, and StampedLock (the optimistic policy) is explicitly not re-entrant and has no Condition support.

variants.name: StampedLock with optimistic read validation (Java 8)
variants.idiom_name: StampedLock stamps with tryOptimisticRead/validate and read/write conversion
variants.implementation_notes: StampedLock is a capability-based policy with three modes: exclusive, shared and optimistic. Acquisition returns a stamp rather than a lock object, so a reader can take an optimistic stamp, copy the state and call validate(stamp), falling back to readLock() plus a re-read when a writer intervened; tryConvertToWriteLock upgrades when no other reader is present. Choose it for read-dominated components where the shared reader state of a ReadWriteLock is the bottleneck, and accept that it does not implement Lock or ReadWriteLock, is not re-entrant, and has no condition variables.
pitfalls: Optimistic reads must be validated after the fields have been copied - validating before reading the state is the classic misuse.
StampedLock is not re-entrant and its locked bodies must not call unknown methods that may re-acquire it (the class is Serializable only, not a Lock), so it cannot replace every policy.
Stamps are opaque long values passed to matching unlock variants; using the wrong stamp is an unchecked error that neither the compiler nor review catches.
